answer.summary: Maples recommends getting out of the present: spend time where the future is already emerging, notice what is missing there, and use those observations—not abstract speculation—to form startup ideas.

sections.heading: Live in the future, then look for what is missing
sections.content: Don’t start by trying to think of a startup. The future already exists in some places today, though it is not evenly distributed. Intentionally get out of the present and ask, “Is this from the future?” More specifically: what part of the future have you actually been living in that gives you grounds to form an opinion about it? Look for unbuilt or missing things in that environment; Maples says noticing those gaps makes your intuition about what to build more likely to be right.

sections.heading: Prepare yourself to notice emerging possibilities
sections.content: Keep thinking about the subject and interact with technologies at the cutting edge; Maples advises actively savoring surprises rather than expecting a recipe for breakthroughs. Look for people or organizations playing offense with new trends—for example, tech-forward early adopters who were excited about cloud products when many others remained skeptical.
